front: Thread visual metaphor: a thread is like a worker in a toy shop. What three qualities do they share?
back:
• Active entity: a worker executes a unit of work for a toy order; a thread executes a unit of work on behalf of a process
  • Works simultaneously with others: many workers build toys at once; threads run concurrently, and on multiple cores at exactly the same time
  • Requires coordination: workers share tools, workstations and parts; threads need coordinated access to platform resources (I/O devices, CPU cores, memory), controlled and scheduled by the OS

front: Process vs. thread: what two components represent a single-threaded process?
back:
• Address space: the virtual to physical memory mapping (code, data, heap)
  • Execution context: CPU registers (including the program counter and stack pointer) and the stack

front: Process vs. thread: where does the OS represent all of a single-threaded process's information?
back: In a process control block (PCB).

front: What do threads of one process share, and what does each thread have its own of?
back:
• Shared: the address space (virtual to physical mapping, code, data, files)
  • Private per thread: its own program counter, stack pointer, registers and stack

front: Why must each thread have its own registers and stack if they share one address space?
back: Because at any given time each thread may be executing a different instruction and accessing a different portion of the shared address space.

front: How does a multithreaded process's PCB differ from a single-threaded one?
back: It is more complex: the thread-specific execution contexts (registers, stack per thread) must be incorporated.

text: Threads run the {{c1::same code}} but each may be executing a {{c2::different instruction}} at any given time.
extra: Same source code, potentially different line or function.

front: Benefits of multithreading: how does parallelism speed up a program?
back: Different threads work in parallel on different components of the workload across multiple processors, so the program finishes faster. Threads can also run completely different portions of the program, e.g. dedicated I/O threads for input processing or display rendering.

front: Benefits of multithreading: what is specialization?
back: Designating certain threads to only certain tasks, so you can manage them specially, e.g. give higher priority to threads handling important tasks or higher-paying customers.

front: Benefits of multithreading: how does specialization help the cache?
back: A specialized thread works on a small subtask, so it can potentially keep more of its state in the processor cache (a hot cache), speeding up repeated execution.

front: Why does a multithreaded app use less memory than a multiprocess app for the same work?
back: A multiprocess app needs a new address space per process; a multithreaded app needs only one address space. E.g. with four CPUs: four processes need four address spaces and four execution contexts; four threads share one address space and need four execution contexts. Less memory means it is more likely to fit in memory and need fewer swaps from disk.

front: Why is inter-thread communication cheaper than inter-process communication (IPC)?
back: Inter-thread communication is primarily reading/writing shared variables, whereas passing data between processes (IPC) is more costly.

front: Single CPU: when is it worth switching to another thread while one waits on a disk request?
back: When t_idle > 2 * t_ctx_switch: the idle time exceeds the time of two context switches (switch away and back), so switching to another thread hides the I/O latency. This makes multithreading useful even on a single CPU.

front: Why does thread context switching create more useful switching opportunities than process context switching?
back: Switching between threads of the same process reuses the same virtual-to-physical mappings, avoiding the costly step of setting up new mappings. Lower switch cost means more cases where switching pays off.

front: What is the benefit of multithreading the OS kernel?
back: It lets the OS support multiple execution contexts that can run concurrently (especially with multiple CPUs), on behalf of applications or OS-level services like daemons and device drivers.
source: Benefits of Multithreading: Apps and OS Code

front: Process vs. thread quiz: do these apply to processes, threads, or both? Can share a virtual address space; take longer to context switch; have an execution context; make use of some communication mechanisms.
back:
• Can share a virtual address space: threads
  • Take longer to context switch: processes (threads share an address space, so switching among them is faster)
  • Have an execution context: both (a stack and registers)
  • Use communication mechanisms: both (IPC for processes; threads have mechanisms to communicate, coordinate and synchronize)
source: Benefits of Multithreading: Apps and OS Code

front: Why do threads tend to produce hotter caches than processes?
back: Threads share the virtual address space, so data one thread needs is often already in cache, brought there by another thread. Among processes, such sharing is not really possible.
source: Benefits of Multithreading: Apps and OS Code

front: What three kinds of support do we need to implement threads?
back:
• A data structure to represent a thread
  • Mechanisms to create and manage threads
  • Mechanisms to let threads coordinate with each other

front: What is a data race?
back: When one thread tries to read data while another modifies it (threads sharing the address space), leading to inconsistencies.

front: What is mutual exclusion, and what construct provides it?
back: A mechanism granting only one thread at a time access to shared data; the rest must wait. It is accomplished with a mutex.

front: What is a condition variable used for?
back: Inter-thread communication: it lets a thread wait on another thread and specify exactly what condition it is waiting on.

text: Mutexes and condition variables are both examples of {{c1::synchronization mechanisms}}.

front: Besides thread creation, mutexes and condition variables, what other mechanisms does Birrell describe that this lesson does not focus on?
back: Mechanisms for waking up other threads from a wait state. The lesson focuses on thread creation and the two synchronization mechanisms (mutexes and condition variables).

front: Thread creation: what information describes a thread?
back:
• Thread ID
  • Program counter
  • Stack pointer
  • Register values
  • Stack
  • Other attributes (e.g. priority)

front: Thread creation: what two arguments does the fork call take (not the UNIX fork)?
back:
• proc: the procedure to run when the thread is created
  • args: the arguments to pass to proc

front: Thread creation: what happens when a thread calls fork?
back: A new thread is created with a new data structure, its program counter pointing to the first instruction of proc, and args on its stack. The parent T0 continues after the fork call; the child T1 starts at the first instruction of proc. Both run concurrently.

front: Thread creation: what two problems arise when a forked thread completes?
back:
• The child needs a way to return its result or communicate its status to the forking thread
  • The forking thread must not exit first, since child threads exit when parent threads do

front: Thread creation: what is one common practice for returning a forked thread's result?
back: Store it in a well-defined location in the address space accessible to all threads, with a mechanism to notify the parent (or another thread) that it is available.

front: Thread creation: what does the join mechanism do?
back: The parent calls join with the child's thread id and blocks until the child finishes. join returns the child's result; when it returns the child exits and its resources are deallocated.

front: Lecture: join returns the child's result to the parent. According to Birrell, how do most forked threads actually deliver results?
back: Most forked threads are daemons or report results by other means; Join is rarely called.

front: Thread creation: besides who joins whom, how do parent and child threads relate?
back: They are completely equivalent: both can access and share all process resources (CPU, memory, any state within the process).

front: Thread creation example: why can we not be certain of the ordering of elements in the list?
back: Nothing guarantees control switches to the child as soon as fork returns, so either the child or the parent may insert its element first; both executions are possible. If safe_insert were not protected, the two concurrent list updates would also be a data race.

front: Thread creation example: in this example when is the join actually necessary?
back: If the child has already finished, join returns immediately. The child's result reaches the parent through the shared list either way, so join is not strictly necessary here. It matters when we need the child's return value or must guarantee the child has finished.

front: Mutexes: walk through the problematic interleaving when threads A and B both insert at the list head.
back: On an initially empty list, A and B both read list and list.p_next (null), and both set their e.pointer to null. A sets list.p_next to its element, then B sets list.p_next to its element, overwriting A's write. Only B's element is linked; A's element is lost.

front: Mutexes: name the two distinct ways the unprotected list insert goes wrong.
back:
• Two threads on one CPU whose operations get randomly interleaved
  • Two threads on two different CPUs updating the pointer field at the same time, with an unknown outcome

front: Mutual exclusion: what happens to a thread that tries to lock a mutex already held?
back: It is blocked on the lock operation and cannot proceed until the mutex owner releases the mutex.

front: Mutual exclusion: what minimum information must a mutex data structure hold?
back:
• Lock status
  • Owner
  • Blocked threads

front: Mutual exclusion: is the list of blocked threads ordered? What follows?
back: No. When the mutex frees, any waiting thread, or a brand new thread just reaching the lock, may acquire it; waiting longer gives no priority. If T3 reaches its lock exactly as T1 releases, T3 may win even though T2 was already waiting.

front: What is a critical section?
back: The portion of code protected by the mutex; it holds code that must be restricted to one thread at a time, commonly read/write access to a shared variable. Only one thread ever executes it at a given moment.

front: Mutual exclusion: what are the two ways a mutex can be unlocked?
back:
• Reaching the end of the clause following a lock statement (Birrell's lock construct, used in the lecture, frees the mutex implicitly at the closing curly bracket)
  • Explicitly calling an unlock function (most common APIs have separate lock and unlock calls)
If an explicit unlock is missed, no other thread can proceed.

front: Mutex example: with T0 inserting 6 and T1 inserting 4 under a mutex, if T0 reaches safe_insert first, what is the resulting list, and does the mutex fix the ordering?
back: The list ends up as 4 -> 6 (T0 inserts 6, T1 blocks, then inserts 4 at the front), but the mutex only guarantees the two inserts do not interleave; the code does not determine which insert happens first.

front: Mutex quiz: T1 holds m. T4 then T2 call lock(m) while T1 holds it, T5 calls lock just as T1 releases, T3 calls lock only after the release. Which threads could get m next, and why?
back: T2, T4 and T5. T2 and T4 are pending, and the mutex gives no guarantee about the order in which pending requests are granted (T4 asking first does not matter). T5 arrives on another CPU while the lock is still free, so it can win. T3 is not a candidate: it asks only after the release, when other requests are already pending.

front: Producer/consumer: why is mutual exclusion alone insufficient here?
back: Mutual exclusion is binary (lock free or not), but the consumer needs to act only under a certain condition, e.g. wait until the list is full. A plain mutex cannot express that condition.

front: Producer/consumer: why is the consumer looping strategy wasteful, and what is the better approach?
back: The consumer busy-loops checking the condition. Ideally the producers should notify the consumer when the list is full instead of having the consumer loop.

front: Condition variables: what must the wait function do with the mutex?
back:
• Release the mutex if the condition is not met, so the signaling thread can acquire it
  • Reacquire the mutex when the condition is met, since wait occurs mid critical section

front: Condition variables: in the producer/consumer example, when does a producer signal list_full, and why must the consumer's wait release the mutex?
back: A producer signals only when its own insert made the list full. While the consumer waits, the only way the list fills is for a producer to acquire the mutex and insert, so wait must release the mutex on entry (and reacquire it on exit, since the consumer then modifies the list).

front: Condition variables: what does the signal function do?
back: A thread holding the mutex calls signal, when the condition becomes true, to alert a waiting thread that it may proceed.

front: Lecture says signal wakes a waiting thread; what does Birrell say about how many it wakes, and why does it matter?
back: Birrell: Signal awakens at least one blocked thread but possibly more; the SRC implementation could rarely wake several. This is one reason he re-checks the condition in a while loop. POSIX pthread_cond_signal likewise unblocks at least one thread.

front: Condition variable API: what should the condition variable data structure contain?
back:
• A mutex reference
  • A list of waiting threads

front: Condition variable API: what do the wait, signal, and broadcast procedures do?
back:
• wait(mutex, cond): release and reacquire the mutex as needed per the condition (atomically release the mutex and join the wait queue; on wake, leave the queue, then reacquire the mutex)
  • signal: tell one waiting thread the condition is met
  • broadcast: tell all waiting threads the condition is met

front: Condition variable API: why is broadcast often not as useful as it seems?
back: Even if broadcast wakes all waiting threads, removing a thread from the wait queue immediately locks the mutex, so still only one thread executes at a time.

front: Lecture is lukewarm on broadcast; what two legitimate uses does Birrell give for it?
back:
• Simplifying a program by waking several threads instead of splitting wait reasons across different condition variables
  • Waking several threads when the just-released resource can serve more than one of them (e.g. readers in a readers/writer lock, who re-acquire the mutex one at a time only to update the counter, then read concurrently)
POSIX recommends broadcast when more than one waiter can proceed; Lampson & Redell treat it as always correct.

front: Condition variable quiz: why does the consumer use while instead of if around wait?
back:
Three linked reasons, all of which apply:
  • it supports multiple consumers: another consumer may get the mutex first and print and clear the list
  • signaling gives no guarantee of access to the mutex once the condition is signaled
  • so the list can change before the woken consumer gets the mutex again
The while re-checks that the condition is actually met on wake-up.

front: What is the readers/writer problem?
back: Some threads want to read shared state and some want to write it. At any time 0 or more readers OR 0 or 1 writers may access it; readers and the writer cannot access it at the same time.

front: Readers/writer: why is wrapping access to the shared state in a plain mutex too restrictive?
back: A mutex allows only one thread at a time, so multiple readers could not read concurrently, which the problem allows.

front: Readers/writer: what do the three conditions on read_counter and write_counter allow?
back:
• read_counter == 0 and write_counter == 0: reading and writing both allowed
  • read_counter > 0: only reading allowed
  • write_counter == 1: neither allowed

front: Readers/writer: how does the single resource_counter encode the three states?
back:
• 0: resource free (reads and writes allowed)
  • > 0: being read; the value is the number of current readers
  • -1: being written (also captures that only one writer can exist)

front: Readers/writer: what is a proxy variable and what does it let a mutex express?
back: A proxy variable (e.g. resource_counter) reflects the state of the resource. Controlling access to the proxy, instead of the state itself, lets a mutex enforce any policy encodable in that variable, not just plain mutual exclusion.

front: Readers/writer example: what four things does the program require?
back:
• resource_counter: proxy variable for the resource state
  • counter_mutex: mutex controlling access to resource_counter
  • read_phase: condition variable, resource ready for reading
  • write_phase: condition variable, resource ready for writing

front: Readers/writer example: what does the last reader do when resource_counter reaches zero, and why signal not broadcast?
back: It signals on write_phase to wake one waiting writer. Only one writer can proceed at a time, so a broadcast is unnecessary.

front: Readers/writer example: why must the woken writer recheck resource_counter != 0 after waking?
back: Removing the thread from the wait queue and reacquiring the mutex are two separate steps. A different thread could acquire the mutex in between and change resource_counter, so the predicate must be rechecked once the mutex is held. Only if resource_counter is still 0 (the != 0 predicate is false) does the writer set it to -1 and write.

front: Readers/writer example: on which condition variable does a newly arriving reader or writer wait, and when?
back:
• Writer arriving while readers or a writer are active: waits on write_phase
  • Reader arriving while a writer is active: waits on read_phase

front: Readers/writer example: when a writer finishes, what does it do with the counter and the condition variables, and why each?
back: It resets resource_counter to 0, then broadcasts to read_phase (multiple readers may read concurrently) and signals write_phase (only one writer may run at a time).

front: Readers/writer example: does calling broadcast before signal control who wakes first?
back: No. The order of calls does not determine which waiter wakes first; the thread scheduler decides, and we usually have no insight into it.

front: Lecture wakes both readers and writers on release; how does Birrell's refined ReleaseExclusive differ?
back: Birrell's refined ReleaseExclusive wakes only one class: it broadcasts to the readers' condition variable if any readers are waiting, otherwise it signals one writer. Waking both classes is correct but is the kind of spurious wake-up his revision removes.

front: Readers/writer example: can several readers hold counter_mutex at once? How then do they read concurrently?
back: No: threads take the mutex one at a time, only to update resource_counter. The reads themselves happen outside the mutex, so after each reader has passed through it in turn, all readers read the shared state concurrently.

front: Critical section structure: where are the real critical sections in the readers/writer app, relative to the mutex?
back: The reading and writing of data are the critical sections, and they sit outside the mutex block; only entering and exiting those operations is governed by the mutex.

front: Critical section structure: what are the common steps each time the mutex is acquired?
back:
• Check a condition; if not met, wait
  • Once met, update the proxy variable
  • If appropriate, signal/broadcast other threads
  • Unlock the mutex

front: Critical section structure: what higher-level operations do the enter and exit blocks correspond to?
back: The "enter critical section" blocks act as a higher-level lock, and the "exit critical section" blocks act as a higher-level unlock, even though a mutex is locked and unlocked inside each.

front: Critical section structure with proxy: what asymmetry exists between the enter and exit blocks?
back: The enter block has a predicate to wait on; the exit block generally has nothing to wait for and just updates the proxy variable and signals or broadcasts. The mutex is held only inside these blocks, so more than one thread can be in the real critical section at once.

front: Common pitfalls: what should you keep track of for each shared resource, and what helps?
back: Keep track of the mutex and condition variables used with a given shared resource. Comments help.

front: Common pitfalls: why must you always acquire the same mutex for a given resource?
back: Using different mutexes to guard one resource provides no mutual exclusion among them, which is equivalent to not using a mutex at all.

front: Common pitfalls: what common mistake occurs when protecting a piece of shared state, and what can help catch it?
back: Forgetting to lock or unlock the mutex associated with that state. Compilers may generate warnings/errors to help.

front: Common pitfalls: besides signal vs. broadcast, what condition-variable mistake can break correctness?
back: Signalling or broadcasting on the wrong condition, e.g. signalling that reads can proceed when you should signal that writes can.

front: Common pitfalls: is confusing signal and broadcast symmetric in consequence?
back: No. Using signal where broadcast is needed is a bug: only one thread wakes, the rest may keep waiting indefinitely, and it can also cause deadlocks. The opposite (broadcast where signal would do) is okay, though it may incur a performance penalty.

front: Common pitfalls: what is the relationship between the order of signal/broadcast calls and thread execution order?
back: None. Execution order is unrelated to the order of signals/broadcasts; if priority or ordering guarantees are needed, other strategies must be devised.

front: What is a spurious wake-up (lecture usage)?
back: Unnecessarily waking a thread when there is no way for it to proceed, e.g. a reader woken by a broadcast tries to acquire the mutex the writer still holds, so it moves from the condition-variable queue to the mutex queue.

front: Spurious wake-ups: do they affect correctness or performance?
back: Only performance: cycles are wasted context switching to threads that are just placed back on another queue. Correctness is unaffected.

front: Lecture calls the woken-then-reblocked thread a "spurious wake-up"; what does Birrell call that case, and what does he reserve "spurious wake-up" for?
back: Birrell calls a thread woken inside Wait only to block on a mutex the signaller still holds a spurious lock conflict. He reserves spurious wake-ups for waking threads that cannot make useful progress (from using Broadcast where Signal would do, or waiting on one condition variable for several reasons). Standard usage (POSIX, OSTEP) is closer to Birrell's sense: returning from wait without the condition being true.

front: Spurious wake-ups: when can you NOT unlock the mutex before signaling or broadcasting?
back: When the signal/broadcast is conditional on some property of the shared state: that property must be read inside the mutex, so the signal or broadcast must also occur within the mutex.

front: Lecture says the signal must stay inside the mutex when it depends on shared state; how does Birrell avoid the lock conflict there?
back: Birrell: only the test of shared state needs the mutex. In ReleaseShared the reader computes doSignal := (i = 0) inside the lock clause and calls Signal(cW) after it, keeping access to i protected while avoiding the lock conflict. POSIX also allows signalling without holding the mutex.

front: What is a deadlock?
back: When two or more competing threads wait on each other to complete, but none of them ever do.

front: Deadlocks: describe the toy shop deadlock example.
back: Two workers each need the single soldering iron and the single solder wire. One grabs the iron, the other the wire; neither gives up what it holds, so neither toy ever gets made.

front: Deadlocks: describe the classic two-mutex deadlock between T1 and T2.
back: T1 locks A then wants B; T2 locks B then wants A. T2 cannot get A (T1 holds it) and T1 cannot get B (T2 holds it), and neither can release what the other needs because both are blocked acquiring.

front: Deadlocks: why does fine-grained locking (unlock A before locking B) not help in the T1/T2 example?
back: Because the operation needs both A and B at the same time, so you cannot release A before taking B.

front: Deadlocks: what is the downside of getting all locks up front (releasing them all at the end) or using a single mega-lock covering both A and B?
back: It may work for some applications but be too restrictive for others: it limits the amount of parallelism in the system.

front: Deadlocks: what is the most ideal prevention solution, and what is paramount about it?
back: Maintain a lock order: every thread acquires mutexes in the same order (e.g. always A before B). The particular order does not matter; consistently enforcing the order throughout the application does.

front: Deadlocks: why does enforcing lock order (always A then B) prevent a cycle?
back: To lock B, a thread must already hold A. If T1 holds A, T2 cannot hold A; if T2 lacks A it has not reached its first lock, so it cannot hold B either. No cycle is possible, so T1 gets B and proceeds.

front: Deadlocks: if lock ordering is foolproof, why are deadlocks still a reality?
back: In a large program with many shared variables and mutexes, especially code from different sources, it is hard to guarantee that every mutex is acquired in exactly the same order across every source file.

front: Deadlocks: what graph condition is necessary and sufficient for deadlock, and what are its edges?
back: A cycle in the wait graph. Edges go from the thread waiting on a resource to the thread owning that resource.

front: Deadlocks: besides lock ordering, what three general approaches deal with deadlocks?
back:
• Prevent: check each lock request for a deadlock; delay it, or restructure the code to release resources first (expensive)
  • Detect and recover: analyze the wait graph for cycles and roll back (expensive; needs enough saved state to recover)
  • Ostrich algorithm: do nothing, hope it never deadlocks, reboot if wrong

front: Deadlocks: why can deadlock recovery via rollback be impossible?
back: Inputs and outputs that came from external sources cannot be rolled back.

front: Deadlocks: why are prevention and detection/recovery not applied everywhere?
back: They impose enough overhead on execution time that they are typically applied only in really performance-critical systems.

front: Critical section quiz: toy shop policy allows up to 3 new orders, and any number of old orders only if at most 1 new order is in progress. What should the new-order entry code wait on?
back: Lock orders_mutex, then wait on new_cond while new_order is 3 (or >= 3), or one new order has already entered and there are old orders in the system; then increment new_order.

front: Critical section quiz: why are the "if" variant and the "old_order >= 0" variant wrong, and why are "== 3" and ">= 3" equivalent?
back:
• if: another thread may change the predicate before the woken thread reacquires the mutex, so it can enter in violation of the policy
  • old_order >= 0: blocks a new order whenever one new order is in, even with no old orders, though up to 3 are allowed
  • new_order never exceeds 3 (it is incremented only after the wait), so == 3 and >= 3 behave identically

front: Kernel vs. user level threads: what are kernel level threads, and who manages them?
back: They imply the OS itself is multithreaded. They are visible to the kernel and managed by kernel components like the kernel level scheduler, which maps them onto physical CPUs.

front: Kernel vs. user level threads: what must happen before a user level thread can execute?
back: It must first be associated with a kernel level thread, and then the OS scheduler must schedule that kernel level thread on the CPU.

front: One-to-one model: what is the mapping and its main benefit?
back: Each user level thread has its own kernel level thread: creating a user level thread either creates a new kernel level thread or associates an existing one with it. The OS sees the threads and understands their needs, so the user library benefits directly from the kernel's multithreading support.

front: One-to-one model: what are its two downsides?
back:
• Expensive: every operation goes to the kernel and pays a system call cost
  • Limited to the kernel's policies and mechanisms (e.g. supported scheduling policies, a limit on the number of threads), which hurts portability: an app with particular thread-management needs runs only on kernels that provide exactly that support

front: Many-to-one model: what is the mapping and its benefits?
back: All user level threads of a process map onto a single kernel level thread, with a user-level library choosing which to run. Benefits: portable, free of OS limits/policies, and no system calls for thread decisions.

front: Many-to-one model: what is the critical downside when a user thread blocks?
back: The OS does not know the process is multithreaded; it sees one kernel thread. A blocking operation puts that kernel thread on a request queue and blocks the entire process, even though other work could proceed.

front: Many-to-many model: what mapping does it allow and what is its benefit?
back: Some user threads are many-to-one and others one-to-one with kernel threads. Benefit: best of both worlds; the kernel knows the process is multithreaded, so if one kernel thread blocks it can switch to another and the process still proceeds.

front: Many-to-many model: define bound vs. unbound threads.
back:
• Unbound: a user level thread can be scheduled on any allocated kernel level thread
  • Bound: a user level thread is always scheduled atop the same kernel level thread

front: Many-to-many model: when are bound threads useful?
back: When a user thread needs better priority or responsiveness to kernel events: the mapping is permanent, so the kernel can schedule the bound kernel thread (and with it the user thread) immediately, e.g. a UI thread when user input arrives.

front: Many-to-many model: what is its main downside, compared with one-to-one and many-to-one?
back: It needs extra coordination between the user level and kernel level thread managers, mostly to exploit performance opportunities. In one-to-one nearly everything goes to the kernel level manager, in many-to-one nearly everything goes to the user level library.

front: Lecture introduces bound/unbound threads in the many-to-many model; how does Stein & Shah describe unbound vs. bound threads?
back: Stein & Shah: unbound threads are multiplexed by the library over a pool of nearly identical LWPs, so any unbound thread can run on any LWP in the pool rather than on one fixed kernel thread. A bound thread is permanently attached to its own LWP.

front: Scope of multithreading: contrast system scope and process scope.
back:
• System scope: OS-level managers look at the whole platform; kernel-visible threads
  • Process scope: a user-level library manages only its own process's threads and cannot see threads outside the process; different processes are managed by different instances of the same library, and some link entirely different libraries

front: Scope of multithreading: process A has twice the user threads of B. How is the CPU split under process scope vs. system scope?
back:
• Process scope: kernel cannot see the threads, so A and B get equal kernel resources (e.g. two kernel level threads each); a thread in A gets half the CPU cycles of a thread in B
  • System scope: threads are kernel-visible, so the kernel allocates CPU relative to the total number of user threads; if its policy is an equal share per user level thread, A gets a larger share overall than B

text: Toy shop order steps: 1 {{c1::accept the order}}, 2 {{c2::parse the order}}, 3 {{c3::cut the wooden parts}}, 4 {{c4::paint and decorate}}, 5 {{c5::assemble the toy}}, 6 {{c6::ship the order}}.

front: Boss/workers pattern: who does what, and what limits throughput?
back: One boss assigns work to worker threads; each worker completes the whole task assigned. Throughput is limited by the boss, and is inversely proportional to the time the boss spends per task.

front: Boss/workers in the toy shop: which steps does the boss do, which do the workers, and why?
back: The boss does only step 1 (accept), passing the order on without looking at what it is for; each worker does steps 2 to 6. This keeps the boss's work per order small.

front: Boss/workers: compare the two ways the boss hands out work.
back:
• Direct signal to an idle worker: no worker-to-worker synchronization, but the boss must track every worker, lowering throughput
  • Shared queue (boss produces, workers consume): boss needs no worker details, raising throughput, but requires synchronization on the queue (workers contend for its front, each item goes to exactly one worker, front and end pointers are compared for full/empty)

front: Boss/workers: which work-assignment approach is usually chosen and why?
back: The shared queue approach. Despite the added synchronization, it decreases the boss's work per task, which increases overall system throughput.

front: Boss/workers: what determines the likelihood of the work queue filling up?
back: The number of workers: with more threads the queue is less likely to be full. If it fills, the boss cannot add items and its time per task increases.

front: Boss/workers: contrast creating workers on demand with a worker pool.
back:
• On demand: create a worker per new task; inefficient if thread creation is costly
  • Pool: workers initialized up front, commonly increased in response to high demand by adding several threads at once rather than one at a time, which tends to be the most effective approach

front: Boss/workers: what are the benefit and the two downsides of the pattern?
back:
• Benefit: overall simplicity
  • Downside: thread pool management overhead, including synchronization for the shared buffer
  • Downside: lacks locality, since the boss does not track what each worker did last

front: Boss/workers worker variants: what is gained by specializing workers by task?
back:
Work can be split by item type, new requests vs. repairs, or class of customer.
  • Locality: each worker accesses only a subset of the state, which is more likely already in CPU cache
  • Better quality of service: more threads for urgent tasks or higher-paying customers

front: Boss/workers worker variants: what does specializing workers by task cost?
back:
• The boss does a little more work deciding which set of workers handles a task, usually offset by the workers now being more efficient
  • Load balancing becomes more difficult to reason about

front: Pipeline pattern: how is work divided, and what does the throughput depend on?
back: The task is split into subtasks, each assigned to a different thread/stage (a six-step process has six kinds of threads; in the toy shop six workers each perform one step); multiple tasks are in flight at different stages. Throughput depends on the weakest (slowest) stage.

front: Pipeline pattern: how do you keep the pipeline balanced when one stage is slow?
back: Allocate more threads to the slow stage; if a step takes three times as long, give it about three times the threads. Thread counts per stage can use the same thread pool technique as boss/workers.

front: Pipeline pattern: why is a shared buffer preferred over direct stage-to-stage handoff?
back: Direct communication couples stages: the earlier stage may wait until the next is free. With a shared buffer a thread deposits output and moves on; the next stage picks it up when ready, correcting small imbalances and avoiding stalls.

front: Pipeline pattern: state the key benefit and the two downsides.
back:
• Benefit: specialization and locality, so state for similar jobs is likely in CPU cache
  • Downside: hard to keep balanced over time as input rate or stage resources change
  • Downside: synchronization overhead at multiple stages

front: Layered pattern: how is work grouped, and how does it differ from a pipeline in direction?
back: Similar subtasks are grouped into a layer; threads in a layer can perform any subtask in it, and a task must pass through all layers. Unlike a pipeline, a task travels up and down through the layers, not in one direction.

front: Layered pattern in the toy shop: how are the six steps grouped into layers?
back:
• Steps 1, 2, 6 (accept, parse, ship): order processing
  • Steps 3, 5 (cut and assemble the wooden pieces)
  • Step 4 (paint and decorate)

front: Layered pattern: give its benefits and downsides.
back:
• Benefit: specialization that is coarser than the pipeline, making the threads-per-layer decision simpler
  • Downside: not suitable for all applications
  • Downside: synchronization is more complex, since each layer must know the layers above and below to receive inputs and pass results

front: Layered pattern: when does grouping steps into a layer actually pay off?
back: Only if the steps in a layer genuinely share state. If they have little in common, assigning them to the same thread gives no locality, and the specialization benefit disappears, e.g. grouping the first and last steps (accept and ship) on one thread.

front: Patterns quiz: with six threads, boss/workers (120ms per toy) vs. a six-stage pipeline (20ms per stage), who wins at 10 orders and at 11 orders?
back: Boss/workers has five workers: 10 orders take two rounds = 240ms, 11 orders take three rounds = 360ms. Pipeline: 10 orders = 120 + 9*20 = 300ms, 11 orders = 120 + 10*20 = 320ms. Boss/workers wins at 10; the pipeline wins at 11. Same metric and thread count, so the better pattern can depend on the input. The calculation ignores synchronization and data-passing overheads, so a real choice needs experimental analysis.
